# Mild traumatic brain injury

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > General trauma > Mild traumatic brain injury*

[Original Article Link](/library/vq0AZh)

---

## Summary

Mild <u>traumatic brain injury</u> (mTBI) is a trauma-induced disruption of <u>brain</u> function on the lowest end of the <u>TBI</u> severity spectrum, typically due to a fall, <u>motor vehicle accident</u>, or <u>sports injury</u>. Characteristic manifestations include a <u>GCS</u> ≥ 13–15, <u>transient loss of consciousness</u>, <u>altered mental status</u> at the time of injury, posttraumatic <u>amnesia</u>, and minor neurological abnormalities that do not require surgical intervention. <u>Concussion</u>, a term often used synonymously with mTBI, is difficult to define but typically refers to a heterogeneous subset of <u>TBI</u> with variable constellations of physical, cognitive, and neuropsychiatric features and variable recovery times. mTBI is primarily a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. <u>Neuroimaging</u> is not routinely indicated, as it is frequently normal or reveals only minor findings that do not alter management. <u>Clinical decision rules</u> for <u>neuroimaging</u> should be used to identify patients at risk of intracranial lesions that require surgical intervention. Most patients with a reassuring clinical presentation can be treated as outpatients after a period of observation, while some benefit from hospital admission and monitoring. If at any point during the observation period the <u>GCS</u> deteriorates to < 13, the patient should be reclassified as <u>moderate TBI</u> or <u>severe TBI</u> and managed accordingly. The mainstay of <u>treatment of mTBI</u> is physical and cognitive rest until patients are completely asymptomatic, followed by a gradual return to activity. Most patients recover completely within 1–2 weeks and better outcomes are associated with early diagnosis and <u>treatment adherence</u>. <u>Postconcussion syndrome</u> is the most common complication, causing symptoms lasting for weeks to months that usually require <u>multidisciplinary care</u> and follow-up.




Athletes with a possible <u>sports-related concussion</u> should be immediately removed from play and assessed by a healthcare professional trained in evaluating these injuries. Sports-specific assessment tools such as the Sport <u>Concussion</u> Assessment Tool (SCAT) may be used. Patients should not be permitted to return to play on the day of injury.




See also “<u>Traumatic brain injury</u>” for information on moderate and <u>severe TBI</u>.

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[10]](/library/ZyYZd7)[[24]](/library/35YSPp)




* mTBI is primarily a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> (See “Clinical features”)

* <u>Neuroimaging</u> is not routinely required.  [[40]](/library/ryYfg7)

* Patients fulfilling <u>criteria for neuroimaging in mTBI</u> should undergo noncontrast CT head as an initial investigation to rule out more severe injuries.

* Follow clinical judgment and local protocols for <u>neuroimaging</u> in patients who do not fulfill the inclusion criteria for validated <u>clinical decision rules</u> (CDRs) for <u>neuroimaging</u>.

* See "Special patient groups” for the approach to patients on <u>antithrombotic therapy</u>.

* Patients with <u>bleeding disorders</u> (e.g., <u>hemophilia</u>): CT head is recommended even in patients with <u>GCS</u> 15 and a normal <u>neurological examination</u>. [[24]](/library/35YSPp)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> can be helpful to evaluate for differential diagnoses or determine bleeding risk (e.g., due to <u>coagulopathy</u>)





### Indications for neuroimaging in mTBI




Various <u>clinical decision rules</u> (CDRs) have been developed to identify when <u>neuroimaging</u> is warranted in mTBI; the choice of CDR varies by institution and guidelines.




#### Adults




Although both of these CDRs have been validated for clinical use, the <u>Canadian CT head rule</u> is recommended.  [[41]](/library/jyY_U7)[[42]](/library/RkWlnl0)




| Adult <u>clinical decision rules for neuroimaging in mTBI</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CDR |  | <br>Criteria for <u>neuroimaging</u>: ≥ 1 of the following<br> | <br>Inclusion criteria: all of the following <br> |
| <br>Canadian CT head rule (<u>CCHR</u>)  [[31]](/library/OyYI27)[[43]](/library/lyYv27)<br> |  | <br><br>* High-risk  <br><br>* <u>GCS</u> score < 15 at 2 hours postinjury<br><br>* Suspected <u>open head injury</u> or <u>depressed skull fracture</u><br><br>* Sign(s) of <u>basilar skull fracture</u><br><br>* ≥ 2 episodes of <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* Age ≥ 65 years<br><br>* Medium-risk <br><br>* <u>Retrograde amnesia</u> ≥ 30 minutes<br><br>* Dangerous mechanism of injury<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>GCS</u> 13–15 and ≥ 1 of the following:<br><br>* <u>Loss of consciousness</u><br><br>* <u>Amnesia</u> to the traumatic <u>head injury</u> event<br><br>* Witnessed <u>disorientation</u><br><br>* Age ≥ 16 years<br><br>* Not on <u>anticoagulants</u> or <u>antiplatelet agents</u><br><br>* No posttraumatic <u>seizures</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>New Orleans criteria [[44]](/library/PyYW27)<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Headache</u><br><br>* <u>Vomiting</u><br><br>* Age > 60 years<br><br>* <u>Alcohol intoxication</u> or drug intoxication<br><br>* Persistent <u>anterograde amnesia</u><br><br>* Signs of trauma above clavicles<br><br>* Posttraumatic <u>seizures</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>GCS</u> 15<br><br>* Normal <u>neurological exam</u><br><br>* History of posttraumatic <u>loss of consciousness</u> or posttraumatic <u>amnesia</u><br><br><br> |





![Canadian CT head rule](media/pmehw90xnk9afpydhnryr0e4.jpg)

Canadian CT head rule




> [!TIP]
> The <u>Canadian CT head rule</u> is used for patients with an initial <u>GCS</u> of 13–15 with or without neurological deficits at presentation. The <u>New Orleans criteria</u> can only be used for patients with an initial <u>GCS</u> of 15 and no neurological deficits at presentation.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Alcohol</u> and substance use alters the <u>GCS</u> score and <u>neurological examination</u>. Intoxication is considered a <u>risk factor</u> for traumatic intracranial lesion (according to the New Orleans Criteria). [[24]](/library/35YSPp)




#### Children [[45]](/library/OzYIG7)[[46]](/library/Kq1Uz30)




* The Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) blunt head-trauma prediction rule is typically the preferred pediatric CDR in US institutions.  [[45]](/library/OzYIG7)[[47]](/library/nq17_30)[[48]](/library/Fs1g9R0)

* Inclusion criteria [[45]](/library/OzYIG7)

* Children ≤ 24 hours after a nonpenetrating clinically relevant <u>head trauma</u> with a <u>GCS</u> ≥ 14

* No known <u>bleeding disorder</u> or neurological disorder that would affect clinical assessment





| <br><u>Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) blunt head-trauma prediction rule</u> [[45]](/library/OzYIG7)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Criterion |  | <br>< 2 years<br> | <br>2–18 years <br> |
| High-risk features | Evidence of <u>skull fracture</u> | <br>* Palpable <u>skull fracture</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Signs of basilar skull fracture</u><br><br> |
| <u>GCS</u> = 14 or other signs of <u>AMS</u> | <br>* E.g., repeated questioning, slow response times to questioning, <u>agitation</u>, <u>somnolence</u><br><br> |  |  |
| Intermediate-risk features | Severe signs or symptoms | <br><br>* Nonfrontal scalp <u>hematoma</u><br><br>* <u>Loss of consciousness</u> > 5 seconds<br><br>* Not acting normally<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vomiting</u><br><br>* Any <u>loss of consciousness</u><br><br>* Severe <u>headache</u><br><br><br> |
| Severe mechanism of injury | <br>* Fall > 3 ft<br><br> | <br>* Fall > 5 ft<br><br> |  |
| <br><br>* Severe <u>motor vehicle crash</u><br><br>* Struck by a motor vehicle as a pedestrian<br><br>* Head struck by high-impact object<br><br><br> |  |  |  |
| <br>Interpretation <br><br>* Any high-risk feature: ∼ 4% risk of clinically important <u>TBI</u>; obtain CT head.<br><br>* Any intermediate-risk feature: ∼ 1% risk of clinically important <u>TBI</u>; consider CT head or observation.  [[45]](/library/OzYIG7)[[49]](/library/6q1jz30)<br><br><br><br> |  |  |  |

> [!WARNING]
> Consider nonaccidental head <u>trauma in children</u> and <u>infants</u>. Perform a thorough history and examine for other signs of abuse. [[50]](/library/iQWJDO0)




### <u>Neuroimaging</u> modalities [[24]](/library/35YSPp)[[51]](/library/EyY8S7)




* CT head without IV contrast

* Indications: preferred initial imaging modality in patients that meet <u>criteria for neuroimaging in mTBI</u> [[10]](/library/ZyYZd7)[[52]](/library/CNbqW8)

* Findings are usually normal; in a minority of patients the following may be seen:  [[40]](/library/ryYfg7)

* Small <u>cerebral contusions</u>: heterogeneous lesions surrounded by <u>cerebral edema</u>.

* Evidence of minimal <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u> (e.g., isolated <u>traumatic SAH</u>) not requiring neurosurgical intervention. [[53]](/library/7MX4JA)

* See also "<u>Diagnostics in TBI</u>" for findings of more <u>severe TBIs</u> and “<u>Differential diagnosis of intracranial hemorrhage</u>” for a comparison of CT findings of <u>intracranial bleeds</u>.

* <u>MRI</u> head

* Indication: second-line imaging modality in patients with clinical features unexplained by CT findings  [[13]](/library/tobXdu)

* Findings: subtle injuries missed on initial <u>CT scan</u> (e.g., microhemorrhages, axonal injury, infarctions) [[54]](/library/l7bvNE)

* Advanced imaging (e.g., susceptibility-weighted imaging, <u>diffusion</u> tensor imaging): may be considered in patients whose clinical features are unexplained by initial <u>neuroimaging</u>





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[10]](/library/ZyYZd7)[[24]](/library/35YSPp)




* In patients with altered consciousness (<u>GCS</u> < 15): investigations to assess for rapidly reversible non-<u>TBI</u> causes of low <u>GCS</u>

* Blood <u>glucose</u>

* <u>Blood alcohol level</u>

* Consider <u>urine toxicology screen</u>  [[55]](/library/dtbocv)

* In patients with suspected <u>coagulopathy</u>: <u>platelet count</u>, <u>coagulation panel</u>
